claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical strength at 1600 °C.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The parent NbMoTaW alloy possesses irradiation resistance.
Introducing approximately 5 at.% V into NbMoTaW can retain a single-phase BCC structure.
Vanadium addition alters local lattice distortions and dislocation-core structures in NbMoTaW.
Vanadium changes the dislocation-solute interaction energy in the modified alloy.
The vanadium-induced changes lower the activation barriers for dislocation nucleation and motion at room temperature.
Easier dislocation nucleation and motion improve plastic deformability and ductility.
Approximately 5 at.% V will significantly increase the room-temperature strain-to-failure relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will retain yield strength and structural stability comparable to untreated NbMoTaW at 1600 °C.
The V-modified alloy will retain irradiation resistance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
Local lattice distortions and compositional complexity can modify irradiation-defect formation energies, migration barriers, diffusion pathways, and recombination behavior.
Similar configurational entropy and retention of the BCC structure are sufficient to prevent degradation of high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance after V addition.
Secondary-phase formation or significant compositional segregation would invalidate the proposed dislocation-based mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as adding V, whereas the conditions describe V substitution; these imply different composition accounting unless the substituted host fractions are specified.

A quintenary alloy containing only 5 at.% V cannot be equiatomic across all five elements. Spatially uniform distribution may be intended, but the stated 'equiatomic distribution with 5 at.% V' is compositionally inconsistent.
